children: From supplier assessments to electric kitchens, Mahindra’s experience highlights the operational and financial complexities behind large-scale emissions reduction

For a large manufacturing group, decarbonisation extends well beyond reducing emissions from its own factories. The harder task is tackling the carbon footprint embedded across suppliers, products and operations that remain outside the company’s direct control.

That challenge is particularly visible in Mahindra Group’s decarbonisation strategy. Advait Padaval, Sustainability Strategy Lead, Mahindra Group, said roughly 95 per cent of the company’s business emissions come under Scope 3, making suppliers and the wider value chain central to its approach.
Beyond The Factory Gate

Mahindra’s sustainability framework covers emissions, energy, water and waste within its own operations. However, Padaval said the company also needs to address emissions generated upstream before components reach its facilities and downstream after products leave the business.

“We do account for a significant portion of the overall India emissions. We account for roughly three per cent of overall India emissions, out of which Scope 3 accounts for roughly 95 per cent of our business,” Padaval said.

The challenge is particularly visible in the tyre industry. Padaval identified tyres among the top three emission factors for Mahindra’s automotive and farm businesses. The company has been engaging tyre suppliers on sustainability, with its procurement scale giving it an avenue to influence discussions around emissions.
The Supplier Problem

Influencing suppliers, however, is different from reducing emissions within a company’s own facilities. Mahindra and Mahindra has more than 2,000 suppliers, Padaval said, with many of them being MSMEs and operating at different levels of ESG maturity.

“To address all of them, it’s a mix. It’s certain larger suppliers, some MSMEs, most of them MSMEs in fact,” he said, underlining the difficulty of applying a uniform approach across the supply chain.

The company’s supplier strategy includes governance, capability building, audits and implementation support. Procurement teams have ESG leads, alongside a dedicated ESG team that works to ensure suppliers understand the company’s ESG requirements.
From Audit To Action
The process goes beyond assessing suppliers. Mahindra’s ESG audits examine energy, emissions, water and waste footprints, with findings used to identify areas requiring intervention.

“The major aspect of our heavy lifting happens in our audits and in the work that we do with our suppliers post that audits,” Padaval said. The company then connects suppliers with solution providers and monitors their progress.

Padaval said Mahindra also supports suppliers financially during the initial stages of implementation. “What is Scope 1 and Scope 2 to them is Scope 3 to us,” he said, explaining why the company works with suppliers on measures beyond its direct operations.

Around 700 suppliers have been assessed over the past three years, according to Padaval. These suppliers contribute more than 60 per cent of Mahindra’s emissions, making prioritisation necessary across its wider supplier base.
When Climate Meets Continuity

The business implications of decarbonisation can also extend beyond emissions. Padaval cited Mahindra Holidays, where around 45 kitchens had been converted to electric equipment, including induction systems and combi ovens.

The initial objective was to address Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. However, Padaval said the transition became particularly relevant when LPG availability emerged as a concern during the Middle East crisis.
“What made it very stark for us was the business continuity benefit of it,” he said, adding that the experience gave the company greater traction when discussing electrification across its processes.
The presentation did not quantify the emissions reduction achieved through the kitchen transition, making it difficult to assess its precise climate impact from the available data.
The Economics Of ESG

For suppliers, particularly smaller businesses, decarbonisation can involve investment and technical constraints. Mahindra’s supplier programme therefore also considers the commercial implications of adopting ESG measures.

Padaval said the company seeks to present sustainability as a business case for suppliers, including through potential cost benefits. “There’s a lot of cost benefit, a lot of other benefits that their businesses realise,” he said.

The approach can also include differential or preferential pricing for suppliers whose practices align with specified parameters. Mahindra has additionally conducted supplier-solution-provider meetings as part of its decarbonisation programme.
Investor interest is another factor. Padaval said he participated in around 25 investor conversations during the previous year, with more than 10 focused on sustainability.

Still, the scale of the challenge remains significant. Padaval acknowledged that Mahindra is “nowhere close to perfect” in its decarbonisation efforts and stressed that companies need to continue making meaningful progress.

The broader challenge for manufacturers is therefore not only reducing emissions within their own operations, but extending that effort across fragmented supply chains where costs, capabilities and levels of preparedness can vary significantly.
The remarks were made during a session on “Decarbonising at Scale: What Worked for Mahindra?” at the 9th Sustainable World Conclave 2026.
